newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece, Turkey make little headway on Aegean Sea.
newsitem.headline: Greece, Turkey make little headway on Aegean Sea.

text.p: Greece and Turkey held to their positions concerning territorial rights in the Aegean Sea on Monday despite calls from both sides to end a climate of mistrust and seek solutions.

Turkish deputy foreign minister Onur Oymen, the first senior Turkish diplomat to visit Greece in years, held talks with his Greek counterpart George Papandreou. Both expressed hope that the two NATO neighbours would find ways to resolve differences.

The two ministers are the architects of the latest effort at rapprochement between Athens and Ankara capitalising on a European Union initiative which calls on two committees of experts -- one from each country -- to seek methods for resolving long standing problems.

At a conference organised by the Athens-based Centre for Political Research, Papandreou said Ankara should take the first step and revoke threats of war against Greece if Athens extends its territorial waters in the Aegean Sea from six to 12 miles.

Greece has this right under international maritime law and has said it will exercise it whenever it sees fit. Turkey says such a move would turn the Aegean, dotted with Greek islands, into a Greek lake and has threatened to strike.

"We respect all international treaties and laws but the Aegean is not the Pacific or the Atlantic Ocean. Such a move would strangle Turkey and you can't expect from any Turkish government or parliament not to react," Oymen said.
"As long as you (Greece) don't change the status quo in the Aegean there is nothing to fear from Turkey," he added.

Oymen called on Athens to start talks over disputed islets near the Turkish coast which Greece considers its territory. Papandreou said that Ankara should go to international courts if it disputed their status.
The two countries came close to war last year over two uninhabited rocks in the eastern Aegean and a clash was averted with U.S. mediation.
Turning to Cyprus, whose northern third has been occupied by Turkish troops since 1974, Oymen said the island could not become a European Union member before Turkey does.

The EU has agreed to start accession talks with Nicosia's internationally recognised Greek-Cypriot government towards the end of the year although many EU members now have second thoughts over such a move before the Greek-Cypriot and Turkish-Cypriot communities reach some common ground.
Papandreou said a letter from the Greek committee of experts would be sent on Monday to the EU's Dutch presidency outlining the Greek positions.

Greece, an EU member, has said it would accept no pressure from the EU to start negotiations and that any rapprochement with Turkey now did not mean Athens would lift its veto within the EU blocking millions of dollars in aid to Ankara.

To lift its veto, Greece wants Turkey to publicly renounce violence as a way to settle disputes, abide by international laws and treaties on existing borders, and agree to use the services of international courts for settling differences.
